doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Music that demands the listener: Stockhausen, Coltrane and pop
summary: Jordan gave Stockhausen a piece played over his music; says serious music is not made to be accepted like pop.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you think that the kind of music you like to play demands more from the listener?

Right it does. I mean Stockhausen, the man pulled in from Bach and Beethoven and them. But I mean the music just got to keep developing man. And you know I’ve played gigs in Germany when Stockhausen, before he got too old, he’d be in the front row. And sometimes he’d had his pad, his notation pad. And one time I took one of his pieces and I played on top of it, I said here, take this, this is how your music will sound. Because his sons, one of them played trumpet and one played baritone sax. And they’d always been on the gig and I said here, give it to him, say here take this, this is the way your music will sound when somebody like this is playing on top of it. But I mean it demands something of it. And it takes a while for some — well I mean look at Coltrane, look how long Coltrane’s been dead. And if you put on some late Coltrane people will start walking out like you’re crazy. I mean right now you know. So how can, you know? And it ain’t about, well see another thing with musicians they want to be accepted by the people. They want to be like a hit. How can you make a hit? How you can accept somebody’s jazz like you accept one of them rappers or one of them, you know one of them pop

people. If you’ve got that in mind you’re not supposed to be in this music. If you want to be accepted like a pop artist and all that. I mean Bird was accepted like a pop artist and all the great players. And Trane was accepted, Ornette’s not accepted like that. But so you just have to realize that you’re trying to do something and maybe in the next fifty years when I’m long dead and gone maybe somebody may say oh man listen to this, and it might be something. You see what I’m saying?
